1.1.1: Om! Reverence to Chandika. Markandeya spoke:
1.1.2: Surya's son Savarni is he who is called the eighth Manu. Hear about his birth, as I tell it at full length,
1.1.3: how by reason of the authority of the Great Illusion that illustrious son of the Sun, Savarni, became the king of the eighth manvantara.
1.1.4: In times ago in the Svarochisha period, a king named Suratha, sprung of the race of Chaitra, reigned over the whole earth.
1.1.5: And while he guarded his subjects duly as if they were his own children, there arose hostile kings, who did not destroy the Kolas.
1.1.6: He, the bearer of a very powerful sceptre, had war with them, and was defeated in war by them, inferior though they were, those non-destroyers of the Kolas.
1.1.7: Then coming to his own city he reigned as king over his own country. That illustrious king was attacked then by those powerful enemies.
1.1.8: His powerful and corrupt ministers, who were evil-disposed to a weak person, thereupon robbed him of treasury and army even there in his own city.
1.1.9: Hence the king, deprived of his sovereignty, departed alone on horseback to a dense forest under the pretence of hunting.
1.1.10: There he saw the hermitage of the noble twice-born Medhas, inhabited by wild animals which were peaceful, graced by the muni's disciples.
1.1.11: And he dwelt there some time, honoured by the muni, roaming hither and thither in that fine hermitage of the muni.
1.1.12: He fell into thought there then, his mind being distraught by selfishness, egotistical: 'Lost indeed is the city which I guarded formerly, and which was guarded by my forefathers.'
1.1.13: 'Whether it is guarded righteously or not by those my servants of wicked conduct, I know not. My chief war-elephant, always ardent,'
1.1.14: 'has passed into the power of my foes; what pleasures will he obtain? They who were my constant followers, favoured with grace, riches and food,'
1.1.15: 'now assuredly pay court to other kings. The treasure which I amassed with great difficulty, squandered continually by those men addicted to unbecoming expenditure,'
1.1.16: 'will go to waste.' These and other matters the king thought of continually.
1.1.17: Near the brahman's hermitage there he saw a solitary vaishya, and asked him, 'Ho! who art thou? and what is the reason of thy coming here?'
1.1.18: 'Why appearest thou as if full of sorrow, as if afflicted in mind?' Hearing this speech of the king, which was uttered in friendly mood,
1.1.19: the vaishya, bowing respectfully, replied to the king.
1.1.21: I am a vaishya, Samadhi by name, born in a family of wealthy folk.
1.1.22: I have been cast out by my sons and wife, who are wicked through greed for wealth; and bereft of riches, wife and sons, my wealth taken by them,
1.1.23: I have come to the forest, unhappy and cast out by my trusted kinsmen. In this state I know not the welfare or misfortune of my sons,
1.1.24: nor the tidings of my family nor of my wife, and here I dwell. Is welfare theirs at home now, or ill-luck?
1.1.25: How are they? Are my sons living good or evil lives?
1.1.27: Those covetous folk, thy sons and wife and others, who have cast thee out from thy wealth—
1.1.28: why dost thou, Sir, fix thy mental affection on them?
1.1.30: This very thought has occurred to me, just as thou hast uttered it, Sir.
1.1.31: What can I do? My mind does not entertain implacability towards those who, abandoning affection for a father, have driven me out in their greed for riches.
1.1.32: My mind, which bears affection as of a master to his family, is affectionate to those very persons. I do not comprehend, although I know it, O high-minded Sir,
1.1.33: how it is that the mind is prone to love even towards worthless kinsmen. On their account my sighs flow and distress of mind arises.
1.1.34: What can I do, since my mind is not relentless to those unloving relatives?
1.1.36: Thereupon they both approached the muni together, O brahman—
1.1.37: the vaishya named Samadhi and the noble king—and having both observed the etiquette worthy of him, as was proper,
1.1.38: they sat down and held various discourse, the vaishya and the king.
1.1.40: Adorable Sir! I desire to ask thee one thing; tell me that,
1.1.41: since it tends to afflict my mind without producing submissiveness of my intellect. Though I have lost my kingdom, I have a selfish feeling for it, even with regard to all the requisites of regal administration,
1.1.42: although I know what it is, yet like one who is ignorant—how is this, O best of munis? And this man has been set at nought and cast off by his children, wife and servants,
1.1.43: and when forsaken by his family he is nevertheless exceedingly full of affection towards them. Thus he and I also are both excessively unhappy;
1.1.44: our minds are drawn by selfish thoughts to this matter, even though we perceive the faults in it. How happens this then, illustrious Sir, that we are deluded although aware of it,
1.1.45: and that this state of delusion besets me and him, who are each blind in respect of discrimination?
1.1.47: Every animal has this knowledge in objects cognizable by the senses,
1.1.48: and an object of sense reaches it thus in divers ways, illustrious Sir! Some living beings are blind by day, and others are blind at night;
1.1.49: some living beings can see equally well by day and at night. Mankind know what is true, but not they alone indeed,
1.1.50: because cattle, birds, wild animals and other creatures all certainly know it; and men have the same knowledge which those wild animals and birds have,
1.1.51: and equally both wild animals and birds have the other knowledge which those men have. Though they have such knowledge, look at these birds,
1.1.52: which, though distressed by hunger themselves, are yet because of that same delusion assiduous in dropping grains into the beaks of their young ones. Human beings are full of longings towards their children, O hero;
1.1.53: do they not pass from greed for self unto mutual benefaction? Dost thou not perceive this? Nevertheless they are hurled into the whirlpool of selfishness, which is the pit of delusion,
1.1.54: through the power of the Great Illusion, which makes worldly existence permanent. Marvel not then at this. This is the contemplation-sleep of the lord of the world,
1.1.55: and the Great Illusion that comes from Hari; by it the world is completely deluded. Verily she, the adorable goddess, the Great Illusion,
1.1.56: forcibly drawing the minds even of those who know, presents them to delusion. By her is created this whole universe, both moveable and immoveable;
1.1.57: she it is who, when propitious, bestows boons on men with a view to their final emancipation. She is Knowledge supreme, the eternal cause of final emancipation,
1.1.58: and the cause of the bondage of worldly existence; she indeed is the queen over all lords.
1.1.60: Adorable Sir! Who then is that goddess whom thou stylest Mahamaya?
1.1.61: How was she born, and what is her sphere of action, O brahman? And what is her disposition, and what is her nature, and whence did she originate, the goddess—
1.1.62: all that I wish to hear from thee, O thou most learned in sacred knowledge!
1.1.64: She exists eternally, embodied as the world. By her this universe was stretched forth.
1.1.65: Nevertheless her origin is in many ways; hear it from me. When she reveals herself in order to accomplish the purposes of the gods,
1.1.66: it is then said in the world that she is born; she is also named the Eternal One. When the universe was converted into absolute ocean, and the adorable lord Vishnu,
1.1.67: stretching Shesha out, wooed the sleep of contemplation at the end of the kalpa, then two terrible Asuras, the renowned Madhu and Kaitabha,
1.1.68: springing from the root of Vishnu's ear, sought to slay Brahma. Brahma the Prajapati stood on the lotus that grew from Vishnu's navel;
1.1.69: and seeing those two fierce Asuras and sleeping Janardana, standing with heart solely thereon intent, in order to awaken Hari, he extolled that Sleep of contemplation
1.1.70: which had made its dwelling in Hari's eyes—the Queen of the universe, the supporter of the world, the cause of permanence and dissolution—
1.1.71: the lord of splendour extolled Vishnu's adorable Sleep, incomparable.
1.1.73: Thou art Svaha, thou art Svadha; thou indeed art Vashatkara, thou hast sound for thy soul;
1.1.74: thou art the nectar of the gods, the two eternal letters; thou existest having the three-fold matras for thy soul; thou existest half a matra in duration, yet eternal, which cannot be uttered specifically;
1.1.75: thou art the Sandhya, the Savitri, thou art the divine mother sublime. By thee indeed everything is maintained, by thee this world is created,
1.1.76: by thee it is protected, O goddess! and thou dost always consume it at the end. At its emanation thou didst take the form of creation, and in protecting it thou hast the form of permanence,
1.1.77: and at the end of this world thou wilt have the form of contraction, O thou who containest the world! Thou art the Great Knowledge, the Great Illusion, the Great Intellect, the Great Memory,
1.1.78: and the Great Delusion, the Lady, the Great Goddess, the Great Demon-queen. And thou art the original source of the universe, the exciting cause of the three qualities;
1.1.79: thou art the Night of the world's destruction, the Great Night, and the Night of delusion, terrible! Thou art Good Fortune, thou art Queen, thou art Modesty; thou art Intelligence characterized by perception;
1.1.80: thou art Shame, Nourishment, and Contentment, Tranquillity and Patience also. Thou art terrible, armed with sword, with spear, with club, and with discus,
1.1.81: with conch, with bow, and having as weapons arrows, slings and an iron mace. Thou art gentle, yea more than gentle, exceedingly beautiful beyond all gentle things;
1.1.82: thou art indeed beyond the highest and the lowest, Queen supreme! And whatever or wherever a thing is, whether good or bad, O thou who art the soul of everything,
1.1.83: thou art the energy which all that possesses. Can I extol thee more than this? By thee, who art such, he indeed who created the world, who protects the world, who consumes the world,
1.1.84: is brought under the dominion of sleep. Who is able here to extol thee? Since Vishnu, I and Shiva
1.1.85: have been made by thee to assume bodies, who then may be powerful enough to extol thee? Being such, do thou, O goddess, lauded thus with thy exalted powers,
1.1.86: bewitch these two unassailable Asuras, Madhu and Kaitabha, and let the imperishable master of the world be lightly brought back to consciousness,
1.1.87: and let him rouse up his intelligence to slay these two great Asuras!
1.1.89: Then the goddess of darkness, extolled thus by the Creator there
1.1.90: in order to awaken Vishnu to slay Madhu and Kaitabha, issued forth from his eyes, mouth, nose, arms and heart and breast,
1.1.91: and stood in the sight of Brahma whose birth is inscrutable; and Janardana, master of the world, being quitted by her, rose up
1.1.92: from his serpent-couch in the universal ocean; and he saw those two then, Madhu and Kaitabha, evil of soul, excelling in heroism and prowess,
1.1.93: red-eyed through anger, fully prepared to devour Brahma. Thereupon the adorable lord Hari rose up and fought with those two,
1.1.94: striking them with his arms, for five thousands of years. And they, exceedingly frenzied with their power, deluded by the Great Illusion,
1.1.95: exclaimed to Keshava, 'Choose a boon from us!'
1.1.97: Be ye both now content with me; ye must both be slain by me!
1.1.98: What need is there of any other boon here? Thus much indeed is my choice.
1.1.100: Gazing then at the entire world, which was nothing but water, those two, who had been thus tricked,
1.1.101: spoke to the adorable lotus-eyed god: 'Slay us where the earth is not overwhelmed with water.'
1.1.103: 'Be it so,' said the adorable wielder of the conch, discus and club; and cutting them with his discus, he clove them both asunder, heads and buttocks.
1.1.104: Thus was she born, when praised by Brahma himself. Now listen again; I tell thee of this goddess' majesty.

2.2.2: Of yore there was a fight for a full hundred years between the gods and Asuras, when Mahisha was lord of the Asuras and Indra lord of the gods;
2.2.3: in it the army of the gods was vanquished by the Asuras who excelled in valour, and the Asura Mahisha, after conquering all the gods, became the Indra.
2.2.4: Then the vanquished gods, placing the lotus-born Prajapati Brahma at their head, went where abode Shiva and Vishnu.
2.2.5: The thirty gods described to them accurately what had happened, the full story of the gods' discomfiture which had been wrought by the Asura Mahisha:
2.2.6: 'He, Mahisha, in his own person domineers over the jurisdictions of the Sun, Indra, Agni, Vayu and the Moon, of Yama and Varuna and of the other gods.'
2.2.7: 'Cast out by that evil-souled Mahisha from Svarga, all the hosts of the gods wander on the earth like mortals.'
2.2.8: 'It has now been related to you both, all that has been wrought by the foe of the Immortals, and we have sought you both as a refuge; let his destruction be devised!'
2.2.9: Having thus heard the words of the gods, Vishnu was wroth and Shiva also; both their faces became furrowed with frowns.
2.2.10: Then issued forth great energy from the mouth of the discus-bearer Vishnu, who was full of intense anger, and from the mouths of Brahma and Shiva;
2.2.11: and from the bodies of Indra and the other gods went forth a very great energy; and it all amalgamated.
2.2.12: The gods beheld the mass of intense energy there like a burning mountain, pervading the other regions of the sky with its blaze;
2.2.13: and that unparalleled energy, born of the bodies of all the gods, which pervaded the three worlds with its light, gathering into one became a female.
2.2.14: By what was Shiva's energy her face was developed, and by Yama's energy grew her hair, and her arms by Vishnu's energy,
2.2.15: by the Moon's her twin breasts; and her waist came into being by Indra's energy, and by Varuna's her legs and thighs, by the Earth's energy her hips,
2.2.16: by Brahma's energy her feet, her toes by the Sun's energy, and by the Vasus' energy her hands and fingers, and by Kuvera's her nose;
2.2.17: and her teeth grew by the Prajapati's energy, and three eyes were developed by Agni's energy;
2.2.18: and her eyebrows were the energy of the two twilights, and her ears Vayu's energy; and the coming into being of the energies of the other gods became the auspicious goddess.
2.2.19: Then gazing at her, who had sprung from the combined energies of all the gods, the Immortals who were afflicted by Mahisha felt a keen joy. Then the gods gave her each their own weapons.
2.2.20: The bearer of the bow Pinaka, drawing a trident forth from his own trident, gave it to her; and Krishna gave a discus, pulling it out of his own discus;
2.2.21: and Varuna gave her a conch, Agni a spear, Maruta gave a bow and a quiver filled with arrows.
2.2.22: Indra, lord of the Immortals, gave a thunderbolt, pulling it out of his own thunderbolt; the Thousand-eyed gave her a bell from his elephant Airavata.
2.2.23: Yama gave a rod from his own rod of Fate, and the lord of the waters a noose; and the Prajapati gave her a necklace of beads, Brahma an earthen water-pot;
2.2.24: the Sun bestowed his own rays on all the pores of her skin, and Destiny gave her a sword and a spotless shield;
2.2.25: and the Ocean of milk a spotless necklace of pearls and also a pair of undecaying garments, and a celestial crest-jewel, a pair of ear-rings, and bracelets,
2.2.26: and a brilliant half-moon ornament, and armlets over all her arms, and also a pair of bright anklets, and a necklet of the finest make,
2.2.27: and rings and gems on all her fingers; and Vishvakarman gave to her a brightly polished axe,
2.2.28: weapons of many shapes and also armour that could not be pierced; and Ocean gave her a garland of fadeless lotus-flowers for her head and another for her breast,
2.2.29: and a very brilliant lotus-flower besides. Himavat gave her a lion to ride on and gems of various kinds.
2.2.30: Kuvera, the lord of wealth, gave a drinking cup ever full of wine. And Shesha, the lord of all the serpents, who supports this earth,
2.2.31: gave her a serpent-necklace adorned with large gems. Honoured by other gods also with gifts of ornaments and weapons,
2.2.32: the goddess uttered a loud roar blended with a horse-laugh again and again. The whole welkin was filled with her terrible roar.
2.2.33: By that penetrating and exceedingly great roar a great echo arose; all the worlds shook and the seas trembled,
2.2.34: the earth quaked and all the mountains moved. And 'Conquer thou!' exclaimed the gods with joy to her who rode on the lion,
2.2.35: and the munis extolled her as they bowed their bodies in faith. Seeing all the three worlds greatly agitated, the foes of the Immortals
2.2.36: uniting all their armies rose up together with uplifted weapons. 'Ha! what is this?' exclaimed the Asura Mahisha in wrath,
2.2.37: and rushed, surrounded by all the Asuras, towards that roar. Then he saw the goddess, pervading the three worlds with her light,
2.2.38: causing the earth to bow at the touch of her feet, grazing the firmament with her crest, shaking the whole of Patala with the twang of her bow-string,
2.2.39: standing pervading the sky all around with her thousand arms. Then began a battle between the goddess and the enemies of the gods,
2.2.40: in which every region of the sky was illumined with the weapons and arms hurled in abundance. The Asura Mahisha's general, the great Asura named Chikshura,
2.2.41: fought with her; and the Asura Chamara, attended by fourfold forces, fought along with others. The great Asura named Udagra with six myriads of chariots fought;
2.2.42: and Mahahanu with a thousand myriads gave battle; and the great Asura Asiloman with fifty millions;
2.2.43: with six hundred myriads Bashkala fought in the battle; another, surrounded with many troops of thousands of elephants and horses,
2.2.44: and with ten million chariots, fought in that battle; and the Asura named Bidala fought in the battle there, surrounded with fifty myriads of myriads of chariots.
2.2.45: And other great Asuras in myriads, surrounded with chariots, elephants and horses,
2.2.46: fought with the goddess in that battle there. Now the Asura Mahisha was surrounded with thousands of ten million times ten millions of chariots and elephants
2.2.47: and horses in the battle there. With iron maces and javelins, with spears and clubs,
2.2.48: with swords, with axes and halberds they fought in the battle against the goddess. And some hurled spears, and others nooses,
2.2.49: but they assailed the goddess with blows from their swords in order to slay her. And then the goddess Chandika those weapons and arms
2.2.50: clove, as it were in merest play, by raining forth her own weapons and arms. The goddess betrayed no exertion in her countenance, while the gods and rishis were praising her.
2.2.51: The queenly goddess hurled her weapons and arms at the Asuras' bodies. The lion also that bore the goddess, enraged and with ruffled mane,
2.2.52: stalked among the armies of Asuras, like fire through the forests. And the deep breaths, which Ambika fighting in the battle breathed forth,
2.2.53: came into real being at once as troops by hundreds and thousands. These fought with axes, with javelins, and swords and halberds,
2.2.54: destroying the Asura bands, being invigorated by the goddess' energy. And of these bands some raised a din with large drums, and others with conchs,
2.2.55: and others besides with tabors, in that great battle-festival. Then the goddess with her trident, her club, with showers of spears,
2.2.56: and with her sword and other weapons slaughtered the great Asuras in hundreds, and laid others low who were bewitched with the ringing of her bell;
2.2.57: and binding other Asuras with her noose, she dragged them on the ground. And others again, cloven in twain by sharp slashes of her sword,
2.2.58: and crushed by blows with her mace, lie on the ground; and some, grievously battered by her club, vomited forth blood.
2.2.59: Some were felled to the ground, pierced in the breast by her trident. Some, being closely massed together, were cut in pieces by the torrent of her arrows in the battle-field.
2.2.60: Following the manner of an army, the afflicters of the thirty gods gave up the ghost; some with their arms cut off, and others with severed necks;
2.2.61: their heads fell from others, others were torn asunder in the middle; and other great Asuras fell to the earth with legs clean cut off;
2.2.62: some were cloven by the goddess into two parts, with a single arm and eye and foot to each part; and others fell and rose again, although with head cut off.
2.2.63: Headless corpses, still grasping the finest weapons, fought with the goddess; and others danced there in the battle, keeping time to the strains of the musical instruments.
2.2.64: Corpses, with heads severed, still held swords and spears and lances in their hands; and other great Asuras were shouting to the goddess, 'Stand! stand!'
2.2.65: With the prostrate chariots, elephants and horses and Asuras the earth became impassable where that great battle took place.
2.2.66: And large rivers formed of torrents of blood straightway flowed along there amidst the armies of Asuras, and among the elephants, Asuras and horses.
2.2.67: Thus Ambika brought that great army of the Asuras to utter destruction in a moment, even as fire utterly consumes a huge pile of grass and timber.
2.2.68: And the lion, with quivering mane, stalked on roaring aloud, prowling as it were for lives out of the bodies of the foes of the Immortals.
2.2.69: The battle was fought there between those troops of the goddess and the Asuras, so that the gods in heaven, sending down showers of flowers, gratified her.

3.3.2: Now the great Asura, the general Chikshura, seeing that army being slaughtered, advanced in wrath to fight with Ambika.
3.3.3: The Asura rained a shower of arrows on the goddess in the battle, as a cloud deluges mount Meru's summit with a shower of rain.
3.3.4: The goddess, cutting asunder the masses of his arrows then as it were in play, smote his horses with her arrows and their charioteer;
3.3.5: and split his bow forthwith and his banner raised high aloft; and with swift missiles pierced his limbs as he stood with shattered bow.
3.3.6: His bow shattered, his chariot useless, his horses killed, his charioteer slain, the Asura armed with sword and shield rushed at the goddess.
3.3.7: With the utmost celerity he smote the lion on the head with his sharp-edged sword, and struck the goddess also on her left arm.
3.3.8: His sword shivered to pieces as it touched her arm, O prince. Thereon, red-eyed with anger, he grasped his pike,
3.3.9: and he, the great Asura, flung it at Bhadrakali, as it were the Sun's orb blazing brightly with its splendour from out the sky.
3.3.10: Seeing that pike falling on her, the goddess hurled her pike, and it shattered that pike into a hundred fragments and the great Asura also.
3.3.11: When he, Mahisha's very valiant general, was slain, Chamara, the afflicter of the thirty gods, advanced mounted on an elephant;
3.3.12: and he also hurled his spear at the goddess. Down to the ground Ambika quickly struck it, assailed with a contemptuous hoot and rendered lustreless.
3.3.13: Seeing his spear broken and fallen, Chamara filled with rage flung a pike; and that she split with her arrows.
3.3.14: Then the lion, leaping up, fastened on to the hollow of the elephant's forehead, and fought in close combat aloft with that foe of the thirty gods;
3.3.15: but both then fell, as they were fighting, from the elephant to the ground. They fought closely locked together with most terrible blows.
3.3.16: Then, quickly springing up to the sky, and descending, the lion severed Chamara's head with a blow from his paw.
3.3.17: And Udagra was slain in battle by the goddess with stones, trees and other things, and Karala also was stricken down by her teeth and fists and feet.
3.3.18: And the goddess, enraged, ground Uddhata to powder with blows from her club; and killed Bashkala with a dart, and Tamra and Andhaka with arrows.
3.3.19: And the supreme three-eyed goddess slew Ugrasya and Ugravirya and Mahahanu also with her trident.
3.3.20: With her sword she struck Bidala's head clean down from his body. She despatched both Durdhara and Durmukha to Yama's abode with her arrows.
3.3.21: Now, as his army was being thus destroyed utterly, the Asura Mahisha in his own buffalo-shape terrified her troops.
3.3.22: Some he laid low by a blow from his muzzle, and others by stamping with his hooves, and others because they were lashed with his tail and gashed with his horns,
3.3.23: and others again by his impetuous rush, his bellowing and his wheeling career, and others by the blast of his breath—thus he laid them low on the face of the earth.
3.3.24: Having laid low the van of her army, the Asura rushed to attack the great goddess' lion. Thereat Ambika displayed her wrath.
3.3.25: And he, great in valour, pounding the surface of the earth with his hooves in his rage, tossed the mountains aloft with his horns and bellowed.
3.3.26: Crushed by his impetuous wheelings the earth crumbled to pieces; and the sea, lashed by his tail, overflowed in every direction;
3.3.27: and the clouds, pierced by his swaying horns, were rent to fragments; mountains fell in hundreds from the sky, being cast down by the blast of his breath.
3.3.28: Chandika looked on the great Asura, as swollen with rage he rushed on, and gave way to her wrath then in order to slay him.
3.3.29: She flung her noose full over him, and bound the great Asura fast. And he quitted his buffalo shape when held bound in the great battle,
3.3.30: and then became a lion suddenly. While Ambika is cutting off his head, he took the appearance of a man with scymitar in hand.
3.3.31: Straightway the goddess with her arrows swiftly pierced the man together with his scymitar and shield. Then he became a huge elephant,
3.3.32: and tugged at her great lion with his trunk and roared, but the goddess cut off his trunk with her sword as he made his tugs.
3.3.33: Next the great Asura assumed his buffalo shape again, and so shook the three worlds with all that is moveable and immoveable therein.
3.3.34: Enraged thereat, Chandika, the mother of the world, quaffed a sublime beverage again and again, and laughed as her eyes gleamed ruddy.
3.3.35: And the Asura roared out, puffed up with his strength and valour and frenzy, and hurled mountains against Chandika with his horns.
3.3.36: And she, shivering to atoms with showers of arrows those mountains that he hurled, spoke to him in confused words, while her mouth was rendered ruddier by the mead that she had drunk.
3.3.38: Roar, roar on thy brief moment, O fool, the while I quaff this mead! The gods shall soon roar, when I shall slay thee even here.
3.3.40: Exclaiming thus she leaped upwards and sat herself on that great Asura, and kicked him on the neck with her foot and struck him with her spear.
3.3.41: And thereupon he, being assailed by her foot, half issued forth from his own mouth in sooth, being completely encompassed by the goddess' valour.
3.3.42: That great Asura, fighting though but half issued forth, was laid low by the goddess, who struck off his head with her great sword.
3.3.43: Then perished all that Daitya army with great lamentation. And all the hosts of the gods rose to the highest exultation.
3.3.44: The gods and the great heavenly rishis poured forth praises to the goddess, the Gandharva chiefs burst into song and the bevies of Apsarases into dances.

4.4.2: When that most valiant evil-souled army of the gods' foes was vanquished by the goddess, Shakra and the hosts of other gods poured forth their praises to her with their voices, reverently bending down their necks and shoulders, while their bodies looked handsome because their hair stood erect with exultation.
4.4.3: The goddess, who stretched out this world by her power, whose body comprises the entire powers of all the hosts of gods—her, Ambika, worthy of worship by all gods and great rishis, we bow before in faith; may she ordain blessings for us!
4.4.4: May she, whose peerless majesty and power the Adorable Ananta, Brahma and Hara cannot in sooth declare—may she, Chandika, to protect the entire world and to destroy the fear of evil turn her mind!
4.4.5: Her, who is Good Fortune herself in the dwellings of men of good deeds, Ill Fortune in those of men of sinful souls; who is Intelligence in the hearts of the prudent, who is Faith in those of the good, and Modesty in that of the high-born man—her, even thee, we bow before; protect the universe, O goddess!
4.4.6: Can we describe this thy thought-transcending form? Or thy abundant surpassing valour that destroyed the Asuras? Or thy surpassing feats which were displayed in battles among all the hosts of Asuras, gods and others, O goddess?
4.4.7: Thou art the cause of all the worlds! Though characterized by the three qualities, by faults thou art not known! Even by Hari, Hara and the other gods thou art incomprehensible! Thou art the resort of all; thou art this entire world which is composed of parts! Thou verily art sublime original Nature untransformed!
4.4.8: Thou, whose complete divinity by means of utterance finds satisfaction in all sacrifices, O goddess, art verily Svaha, and givest satisfaction to the Pitri-hosts! Hence thou art in truth declared by men to be Svadha also.
4.4.9: Thou art she who effects final emancipation, and performs great thought-transcending penances! Thou art studied by munis who seek final emancipation, who have shed all their faults, with their organs, which are the essence of strength, well-restrained! Thou art The Knowledge, adorable, sublime in sooth, O goddess!
4.4.10: Sound is thy soul! Thou art the repository of the most spotless ric and yajus hymns, and of the samans, which have the charming-worded texts of the Udgitha! Thou as goddess art the triple Veda, the adorable, and for the existence and production of all the worlds art active; thou art the supreme destroyer of their pains!
4.4.11: Thou art Mental Vigour, O goddess! Thou hast comprehended the essence of all the Scriptures! Thou art Durga, the boat to cross the difficult ocean of existence, devoid of attachments! Thou art Shri, who has planted her dominion alone in the heart of Kaitabha's foe! Thou indeed art Gauri, who has fixed her dwelling in the moon-crested god!
4.4.12: Slightly smiling, spotless, resembling the full moon's orb, beautiful as the choicest gold, and lovely was thy face! Yet it was very marvellous that, being swayed by anger, the Asura Mahisha suddenly smote thy face when he saw it.
4.4.13: But after seeing thy wrathful face, O goddess, terrible with its frowns, and sheeny in hue like the rising moon, that Mahisha did not forthwith yield up his life—it was passing wonderful! For who can live after beholding the King of Death enraged?
4.4.14: Be gracious, O goddess, as supreme lady, to life! When enraged thou dost forthwith destroy whole families! Known at this very moment is this, that here is brought to its end the Asura Mahisha's most extensive might!
4.4.15: Esteemed are they among the nations, theirs are riches, theirs are glories, and their sum of righteousness perishes not; happy are they indeed, and they possess devoted children, servants and wives, on whom thou, well-pleased, dost always bestow prosperity, O lady!
4.4.16: All righteous actions ever indeed, O goddess, with utmost respect the man of good deeds daily performs, and gains heaven thereafter by thy favour, O lady. Dost thou not by him bestow rewards even on the three worlds, O goddess?
4.4.17: Thou, O Durga, when called to mind, dost remove terror from every creature! Thou, when called to mind by those in health, dost bestow a mind extremely bright! What goddess but thou, O dispeller of poverty, pain and fear, has ever benevolent thoughts in order to work benefits to all?
4.4.18: By these slain foes the world attains to happiness; thus let these forsooth practise sin so as to descend to hell for long! 'Meeting death in battle let them proceed to heaven'—thinking thus, thou dost assuredly destroy the enemies, O goddess!
4.4.19: Having indeed seen them, why dost thou not, O lady, reduce to ashes all the Asuras, since thou directest thy weapons against the foes? 'Let even enemies, purified by dying in arms, attain in sooth to the bright worlds'—such is thy most kindly intention towards even them.
4.4.20: And though, neither by the sharp flashes of abundant light from thy scymitar, nor by the copious lustre of thy spear-point, the eyes of the Asuras were destroyed; yet, as they gazed upon thy countenance which bore a portion of the radiant moon, this very thing happened.
4.4.21: Thy disposition, O goddess, subdues the conduct of men of evil conduct; and this thy form surpasses thought and rivalry by others; and thy valour vanquishes those who have robbed the gods of their prowess; thou hast as it were manifested pity thus even on enemies!
4.4.22: To what may this thy prowess be compared? And whereto thy form most charming, which strikes fear among foes? Compassion in mind and relentlessness in battle are seen in thee, O goddess, who bestowest boons even on the three worlds!
4.4.23: Through the destruction of the foes, these three worlds entire have been saved by thee. Having slain them in the battle-front, thou hast led even those hosts of foes to heaven, and dispelled the fear which beset us from the frenzied foes of the gods. Reverence to thee!
4.4.24: With thy spear protect us, O goddess! Protect us with thy sword also, O Ambika! By the clanging of thy bell protect us, and by the twanging of the thong of thy bow!
4.4.25: In the east guard us, and in the west; O Chandika, guard us in the south by the brandishing of thy spear, and also in the north, O goddess!
4.4.26: Whatever gentle forms of thee wander about in the three worlds, and whatever exceedingly terrible forms wander, by means of them guard us and the earth!
4.4.27: Thy sword and spear and club, and whatever other weapons, O Ambika, rest in thy pliant hand, with them guard us on every side!
4.4.29: Thus was she, the Upholder of the worlds, hymned by the gods, and they paid honour to her with celestial flowers that blossomed in Nandana, and with perfumes and unguents.
4.4.30: Moreover all the thirty gods in faith censed her with heavenly incenses. Benignly sweet in countenance, she spoke to all the prostrate gods.
4.4.32: Choose, ye thirty all, whatever ye desire of me, for I grant it with pleasure, being highly honoured by these hymns.
4.4.34: Thou, O adorable lady, hast accomplished all; nought remains undone,
4.4.35: in that this Asura Mahisha, our foe, has been slain. Yet if thou must grant us a boon, O great goddess,
4.4.36: whenever we call thee to mind, do thou away with our direst calamities! And whatever mortal shall praise thee with these hymns, O lady of spotless countenance,
4.4.37: to prosper him in wealth and wife and other blessings by means of riches, success and power, do thou incline always, O Ambika, who art propitious to us!
4.4.39: Being thus propitiated by the gods for the good of the world and on their own behalf, 'Be it so!' said she, Bhadrakali, and vanished from their sight, O king.
4.4.40: Thus I have narrated this, O king, how the goddess came into being of yore from out of the gods' bodies, she who desires the good of all the three worlds.
4.4.41: And again she came into existence, having the body of Gauri, just as she did before, in order to slay the wicked Daityas and Shumbha and Nishumbha,
4.4.42: and to preserve the worlds, as benefactress of the gods. Hearken then to what I have declared to thee; I have truly told it thee.

5.5.2: Of yore the Asuras Shumbha and Nishumbha, trusting in their pride and strength, robbed Shachi's lord of the three worlds and of his portions of the sacrifices;
5.5.3: they both usurped likewise the sun's dignity and the moon's dominion, and Kuvera's and Yama's and Varuna's;
5.5.4: and they both exercised Vayu's authority and Agni's sphere of action. Thereby the gods were scattered, deprived of their sovereignties and put to rout.
5.5.5: The thirty gods, bereft of their dominion and set at nought by those two great Asuras, all recall to mind that never-vanquished goddess:
5.5.6: 'Thou didst grant us the boon—As ye, when in calamities, shall call me to mind, that very moment will I put an end to all your direst calamities.'
5.5.7: Making this resolve, the gods went to Himavat, lord among mountains, and there raised their hymn to the goddess, who is Vishnu's illusive power.
5.5.9: Reverence to the goddess, to the great goddess! To her who is auspicious reverence perpetually! Reverence to Prakriti the good! Submissive we fall prostrate before her!
5.5.10: Reverence to her who is terrible, to her who is constant! To Gauri, to Dhatri reverence, yea reverence! And to the Moonlight, to her who has the moon's form, to her who is happy, reverence continually!
5.5.11: Falling prostrate, to her who is propitious, to Prosperity, to Perfection let us pay reverence, yea reverence! To Nirriti, to the goddess of Good Fortune of kings, to thee, Sharvani, reverence, yea reverence!
5.5.12: To Durga, to her who is a further shore difficult to be reached, to her who is essential, to her who works all things, and to Fame also, to her who is blue-black, to her who is smoke-dark, reverence continually!
5.5.13: Before her who is at once most gentle and most harsh we fall prostrate; to her reverence, yea reverence! Reverence to her who is the foundation of the world! To the goddess who is Action reverence, yea reverence!
5.5.77: To the goddess who among all created beings is called Vishnu's illusive power—reverence to her, reverence to her, reverence to her, reverence, yea reverence! To the goddess who among all created beings bears the name Consciousness—reverence to her, reverence to her, reverence to her, reverence, yea reverence! To the goddess who among all created beings stands firm with the form of Intellect—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Sleep—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Hunger—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Shadow—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Energy—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Thirst—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Patience—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Speciality—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Modesty—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Peaceableness—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Faith—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Loveliness—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Good Fortune—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Activity—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Memory—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Mercy—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Contentment—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Mother—reverence to her, yea reverence! To the goddess who stands firm with the form of Error—reverence to her, yea reverence! To her who both governs the organs of sense of created beings, and rules among all created beings perpetually—to her, the goddess of Pervasiveness, reverence, yea reverence!
5.5.81: To her who exists pervading this entire world with the form of Thinking Mind—reverence to her, reverence to her, reverence to her, reverence, yea reverence! Praised by the gods aforetime because of eagerly-desired protection, and waited upon by the lord of the gods many days, may she, the goddess, the origin of brightness, accomplish for us bright things, yea good things, and ward off calamities!
5.5.82: And she, who is both reverenced as queen by us gods, who are tormented now by the arrogant Daityas, and whom we call to mind as we bow our bodies in faith, she this very moment destroys all our calamities!
5.5.84: While the gods were thus engaged in offering hymns and other reverential acts, Parvati came there to bathe in the water of the Ganges, O prince.
5.5.85: She, the beautiful-browed, said to those gods, 'Whom do ye, lords, hymn here?' And springing forth from the treasure-house of her body, the auspicious goddess spoke:
5.5.86: 'For me this hymn is uttered by the assembled gods, who have been set at nought by the Daitya Shumbha and routed in battle by Nishumbha.'
5.5.87: Because Ambika issued forth from the treasure-house of Parvati's body, she is therefore named in song as Kaushiki among all the worlds.
5.5.88: Now after she had issued forth, the other also, even Parvati, became black; she is celebrated as Kalika; she fixed her abode on Mount Himavat.
5.5.89: Thereafter Chanda and Munda, the two servants of Shumbha and Nishumbha, saw Ambika displaying her sublime and most captivating form;
5.5.90: and both spake out unto Shumbha: 'What woman then, most surpassingly captivating, dwells here, illuminating Mount Himavat, O great king?'
5.5.91: 'Such sublime beauty was never in sooth seen by anyone anywhere; let it be ascertained if she is any goddess, and let her be taken possession of, O lord of the Asuras.'
5.5.92: 'A gem among women, surpassingly beautiful in body, illuminating the regions of the sky with her lustre—there she is then, O lord of the Daityas; deign, Sir, to look at her.'
5.5.93: 'Moreover, whatever gems, precious stones, elephants, horses and other valuable things indeed exist in the three worlds, O lord, all those display their splendour at this present time in thy house.'
5.5.94: 'Airavata, gem among elephants, has been captured from Purandara; and this Parijata tree and also the horse Uchchaihshravas.'
5.5.95: 'Here stands the heavenly chariot yoked with swans in thy court-yard; it has been brought here, the wonderful chariot composed of gems, which belonged to Brahma.'
5.5.96: 'Here is the Nidhi Mahapadma, captured from the Lord of wealth. And the Ocean gave a garland made of filaments and of undying lotus flowers.'
5.5.97: 'In thy house stands Varuna's umbrella, which streams with gold. And here is the choice chariot that belonged to Prajapati formerly.'
5.5.98: 'Thou, O lord, hast carried off Death's power, which is named Utkranti-da. The noose of the Ocean-king is in thy brother's possession.'
5.5.99: 'And Nishumbha has every kind of gem which is produced in the sea. Agni also gave thee two garments which are purified by fire.'
5.5.100: 'Thus, O lord of the Daityas, all gems have been captured by thee; why dost thou not seize this auspicious lady, this gem of womankind?'
5.5.102: Shumbha, on hearing this speech then from Chanda and Munda, sent the great Asura Sugriva as messenger to the goddess,
5.5.103: saying, 'Go and address her thus and thus according to my words, and lightly conduct the matter so that she may come to me of her own good pleasure.'
5.5.104: He went to where the goddess sat on a very bright spot in the mountain, and spoke gently with mellifluous voice.
5.5.106: O goddess! Shumbha, lord of the Daityas, is supreme lord over the three worlds. A messenger am I, sent by him; to thy presence here I have come.
5.5.107: Hearken to what he has said, whose command is never resisted among all beings of divine origin, and who has vanquished every foe of the Daityas:
5.5.108: 'Mine are all the three worlds; obedient to my authority are the gods; I eat every portion of the sacrifices separately.'
5.5.109: 'The choicest gems in the three worlds are altogether under my power; and so is the finest of elephants, the chariot-beast of the lord of the gods, since I have captured it.'
5.5.110: 'That gem among horses, named Uchchaihshravas, which came forth at the churning of the sea of milk, was presented to me by the immortals who prostrated themselves before me.'
5.5.111: 'And whatever other created things in the shape of gems existed among the gods, Gandharvas and Nagas, they were presented even to me, O brilliant lady.'
5.5.112: 'I esteem thee, O goddess, to be the gem of womankind in the world; do thou, who art such, approach unto me, since I am an enjoyer of gems.'
5.5.113: 'Either to me, or to my younger brother Nishumbha of wide-reaching prowess, approach thou, O lady of quick side-glances, since thou art in truth a gem.'
5.5.114: 'Supreme dominion beyond compare thou shalt gain by wedding me. Understand and consider this, and come unto wedlock with me.'
5.5.116: Thus accosted, the goddess, smiling deeply within herself—she, Durga the adorable and good, who supports this world—sang this reply then.
5.5.118: Truly hast thou spoken; nought hast thou uttered falsely herein. Sovereign of the three worlds is Shumbha, and like unto him is Nishumbha also!
5.5.119: But how can that which has been promised concerning this myself be fulfilled falsely? Hearken, what vow I made formerly by reason of my small understanding at that time:
5.5.120: 'He who vanquishes me in fight, who forces my pride from me, and who is my match in strength in the world, he shall be my husband.'
5.5.121: Let Shumbha come here then, or Nishumbha the great Asura; let him vanquish me—what need of delay here?—and let him lightly take my hand in marriage!
5.5.123: Proud art thou! Talk not so before me, O goddess! What male in the three worlds may stand front to front with Shumbha and Nishumbha?
5.5.124: All the gods verily stand not face to face with even the other Daityas in battle, O goddess; how much less canst thou so stand, a woman single-handed!
5.5.125: With Shumbha and those other Daityas, against whom Indra and all the other gods stood not in battle, how shalt thou, a woman, venture face to face?
5.5.126: Do thou, being such, to whom I have in sooth delivered my message, go near unto Shumbha and Nishumbha; let it not be that thou shalt go with thy dignity shattered, in that thou wilt be dragged thither by thy hair!
5.5.128: So strong as this is Shumbha! and so exceedingly heroic is Nishumbha! What can I do, since there stands my ill-considered promise of long ago?
5.5.129: Go thou thyself; make known respectfully to the lord of the Asuras all this that I have said to thee, and let him do whatever is fitting.

6.6.2: The messenger, on hearing this speech from the goddess, was filled with indignation, and approaching related it fully to the Daitya king.
6.6.3: The Asura monarch then, after hearing that report from his messenger, was wroth and commanded Dhumralochana, a chieftain of the Daityas:
6.6.4: 'Ho! Dhumralochana, haste thee together with thy army; fetch by force that shrew, who will be unnerved when dragged along by her hair.'
6.6.5: 'Or if any man besides stands up to offer her deliverance, let him be slain, be he an Immortal, a Yaksha or a Gandharva forsooth.'
6.6.7: Thereupon at his command the Daitya Dhumralochana went forthwith quickly, accompanied by sixty thousand Asuras.
6.6.8: On seeing the goddess stationed on the snowy mountain, he cried aloud to her there: 'Come forward to the presence of Shumbha and Nishumbha;'
6.6.9: 'if thou wilt not, lady, approach my lord with affection now, I will here take thee by force, who wilt be unnerved since thou shalt be dragged along by thy hair!'
6.6.11: Sent by the king of the Daityas, mighty thyself, and accompanied by an army, thou dost thus take me by force—then what can I do unto thee?
6.6.13: At this reply the Asura Dhumralochana rushed towards her. Then Ambika with a mere roar reduced him to ashes.
6.6.14: And the great army of Asuras, enraged, poured on Ambika a shower both of sharp arrows and of javelins and axes.
6.6.15: The lion that carried the goddess, shaking his mane in anger and uttering a most terrific roar, fell on the army of Asuras;
6.6.16: he slaughtered some Asuras with a blow from his forepaw, and others with his mouth, and others, very great Asuras, by striking them with his hind foot.
6.6.17: The lion with his claws tore out the entrails of some, and struck their heads off with a cuff-like blow.
6.6.18: And he severed arms and heads from others, and shaking his mane drank the blood that flowed from the entrails of others.
6.6.19: In a moment all that army was brought to destruction by the high-spirited lion, who bore the goddess and who was enraged exceedingly.
6.6.20: When he heard that that Asura Dhumralochana was slain by the goddess, and all his army besides was destroyed by the goddess' lion,
6.6.21: Shumbha, the lord of the Daityas, fell into a rage and his lip quivered greatly, and he commanded the two mighty Asuras Chanda and Munda:
6.6.22: 'Ho, Chanda! Ho, Munda! take with you a multitude of troops and go there; and going there bring her here speedily,'
6.6.23: 'dragging her by her hair or binding her; if ye have a doubt of that, then let her be slain outright in fight by all the Asuras brandishing all their weapons.'
6.6.24: 'When that shrew is slain and her lion stricken down, seize her, Ambika, bind her and bring her quickly!'

7.7.2: Then at his command the Daityas, led by Chanda and Munda, and arrayed in the four-fold order of an army, marched with weapons uplifted.
7.7.3: Soon they saw the goddess, slightly smiling, seated upon the lion, on a huge golden peak of the majestic mountain.
7.7.4: On seeing her, some of them made a strenuous effort to capture her, and others approached her holding their bows bent and their swords drawn.
7.7.5: Thereat Ambika uttered her wrath aloud against those foes, and her countenance then grew dark as ink in her wrath.
7.7.6: Out from the surface of her forehead, which was rugged with frowns, issued suddenly Kali of the terrible countenance, armed with a sword and noose,
7.7.7: bearing a many-coloured skull-topped staff, decorated with a garland of skulls, clad in a tiger's skin, very appalling because of her emaciated flesh,
7.7.8: exceedingly wide of mouth, lolling out her tongue terribly, having deep-sunk reddish eyes, and filling the regions of the sky with her roars.
7.7.9: She fell upon the great Asuras impetuously, dealing slaughter among the host, and devoured that army of the gods' foes there.
7.7.10: Taking up the elephants with one hand she flung them into her mouth, together with their rearmen and drivers and their warrior-riders and bells.
7.7.11: Flinging likewise warrior with his horses, and chariot with its driver into her mouth, she ground them most frightfully with her teeth.
7.7.12: She seized one by the hair, and another by the neck; and she kicked another with her foot, and crushed another against her breast.
7.7.13: And she seized with her mouth the weapons and the great arms which those Asuras abandoned, and crunched them up with her teeth in her fury.
7.7.14: She crushed all that host of mighty and high-spirited Asuras; and devoured some and battered others.
7.7.15: Some were slain with her sword, some were struck with her skull-topped staff, and other Asuras met their death being wounded with the edge of her teeth.
7.7.16: Seeing all that host of Asuras laid low in a moment, Chanda rushed against her, Kali, who was exceedingly appalling.
7.7.17: Munda the great Asura covered her, the terrible-eyed goddess, with very terrible showers of arrows and with discuses hurled in thousands.
7.7.18: Those discuses seemed to be penetrating her countenance in multitudes, like as very many solar orbs might penetrate the body of a thunder-cloud.
7.7.19: Thereat Kali, who was roaring frightfully, laughed terribly with excessive fury, showing the gleam of her unsightly teeth within her dreadful mouth.
7.7.20: And the goddess, mounting upon her great lion, rushed at Chanda, and seizing him by his hair struck off his head with her sword.
7.7.21: And Munda also rushed at her when he saw Chanda laid low; him also she felled to the ground, stricken with her scymitar in her fury.
7.7.22: Then the army, so much as escaped unslain, seeing Chanda laid low and most valiant Munda also, seized with panic fled in all directions.
7.7.23: And Kali, holding Chanda's head and Munda also, approached Chandika and said, her voice mingled with passionate loud laughter:
7.7.24: 'Here I have brought thee Chanda and Munda, two great beasts; thou thyself shalt slay Shumbha and Nishumbha in the battle-sacrifice.'
7.7.26: Thereon, seeing those two great Asuras Chanda and Munda brought to her, auspicious Chandika spoke to Kali this witty speech:
7.7.27: 'Because thou hast seized both Chanda and Munda and brought them, thou, O goddess, shalt therefore be famed in the world by the name Chamunda!'

8.8.2: After both the Daitya Chanda was slain and Munda was laid low, and many soldiers were destroyed, the lord of the Asuras,
8.8.3: majestic Shumbha, with mind overcome by wrath, gave command then to array all the Daitya hosts:
8.8.4: 'Now let the eighty-six Daityas, upraising their weapons, march forth with all their forces; let the eighty-four Kambus march forth surrounded by their own forces;'
8.8.5: 'let the fifty Asura families who excel in valour go forth; let the hundred families of Dhaumra go forth at my command.'
8.8.6: 'Let the Kalakas, the Daurhritas, the Mauryas, and the Kalakeyas—let these Asuras, hastening at my command, march forth ready for battle.'
8.8.7: After issuing these commands, Shumbha, the lord of the Asuras, who ruled with fear, went forth, attended by many thousands of great soldiers.
8.8.8: Chandika, seeing that most terrible army at hand, filled the space between the earth and the firmament with the twanging of her bow-string.
8.8.9: Thereon her lion roared exceedingly loud, O king; and Ambika augmented those roars with the clanging of her bell.
8.8.10: Kali, filling the regions of the sky with the noise from her bow-string, from the lion and from the bell, and expanding her mouth wide with her terrific roars, had the predominance.
8.8.11: On hearing that roar, the Daitya armies, enraged, surrounded on all four sides the goddess, the lion and Kali.
8.8.12: At this moment, O king, in order to destroy the gods' foes, and for the well-being of the lion-like Immortals, there issued forth, endowed with excessive vigour and strength,
8.8.13: the Energies from the bodies of Brahma, Shiva, Guha and Vishnu and of Indra also, and went in the forms of those gods to Chandika.
8.8.14: Whatever was the form of each god, and whatever his ornaments and vehicle, in that very appearance his Energy advanced to fight with the Asuras.
8.8.15: In the front of a heavenly car drawn by swans advanced Brahma's Energy, bearing a rosary of seeds and an earthen water-pot; she is called Brahmani.
8.8.16: Maheshvara's Energy, seated on a bull, grasping a fine trident, and wearing a girdle of large snakes, arrived, adorned with a digit of the moon.
8.8.17: And Kumara's Energy, Ambika, with spear in hand and riding on a choice peacock, advanced in Guha's shape to attack the Daityas.
8.8.18: Likewise Vishnu's Energy, seated upon Garuda, advanced with conch, discus, club, bow and scymitar in hand.
8.8.19: The Energy of Hari, who assumes the peerless form of a sacrificial boar, she also advanced there, assuming a boar-like form.
8.8.20: Narasimha's Energy, assuming a body like Nrisimha's, arrived there, adorned with a cluster of constellations hurled down by the tossing of his mane.
8.8.21: Likewise Indra's Energy, with thunderbolt in hand, seated upon the lord of elephants and having a thousand eyes, arrived; as is Shakra, such indeed was she.
8.8.22: Then Shiva, surrounded by those Energies of the gods, said to Chandika, 'Let the Asuras be slain forthwith through my good-will.'
8.8.23: Thereupon from the goddess' body there came forth Chandika's Energy, most terrific, exceedingly fierce, howling like a hundred jackals.
8.8.24: And she, the unconquered, said to Shiva, who was smoke-coloured and had matted locks, 'Be thou, my lord, a messenger to the presence of Shumbha and Nishumbha.'
8.8.25: 'Say unto the two overweening Danavas, Shumbha and Nishumbha, and to whatever other Danavas are assembled there to do battle:'
8.8.26: 'Let Indra obtain the three worlds, let the gods be the enjoyers of the oblations; go ye to Patala if ye wish to live.'
8.8.27: 'Yet if through pride in your strength ye are longing for battle, come ye on then! Let my jackals be glutted with your flesh.'
8.8.28: Because the goddess appointed Shiva himself to be ambassador, she has hence attained fame as Shivaduti in this world.
8.8.29: Those great Asuras however, on hearing the goddess' speech fully announced, were filled with indignation and went where Katyayani stood.
8.8.30: Then, at the very first, the arrogant and indignant foes of the Immortals in front poured on the goddess showers of arrows, javelins and spears.
8.8.31: And gracefully she clove those arrows, darts, spears and axes, which were hurled, with large arrows shot from her resounding bow.
8.8.32: And in front of her stalked Kali then, tearing the foes asunder with the onset of her darts and crushing them with her skull-topped staff.
8.8.33: And Brahmani caused the foes to lose their courage by casting water on them from her earthen pot, and weakened their vigour, by whatever way she ran.
8.8.34: Maheshvara's Energy slew Daityas with her trident, and Vishnu's Energy with her discus, and Kumara's Energy, very wrathful, slew them with her javelin.
8.8.35: Torn to pieces by the down-rush of the thunderbolt hurled by Indra's Energy, Daityas and Danavas fell on the earth in hundreds, pouring out streams of blood.
8.8.36: Shattered by the boar-embodied Energy with blows from her snout, wounded in their breasts by the points of her tushes, and torn by her discus, demons fell down.
8.8.37: And Narasimha's Energy roamed about in the battle, devouring other great Asuras who were torn by her claws, as she filled the intermediate region of the sky with her roaring.
8.8.38: Asuras, demoralized by Shivaduti with her violent loud laughs, fell down on the earth; she then devoured those fallen ones.
8.8.39: Seeing the enraged band of Mothers crushing the great Asuras thus by various means, the troops of the gods' foes perished.
8.8.40: Raktavija, a great Asura, seeing the Daityas, who were hard-pressed by the band of Mothers, intent on fleeing, strode forward to fight in wrath.
8.8.41: When from his body there falls to the ground a drop of blood, at that moment starts up from the earth an Asura of his stature.
8.8.42: He, a great Asura, with club in hand, fought with Indra's Energy, and Indra's Energy then struck Raktavija with her thunderbolt;
8.8.43: blood flowed quickly from him when wounded by the thunderbolt. Thereupon stood up together fresh combatants, like him in body, like him in valour;
8.8.44: for as many blood-drops fell from his body, so many men came into being, like him in courage, strength and valour.
8.8.45: And those men also who sprang from his blood fought there with the Mothers in a combat, dreadful because of the sweep of their very sharp weapons.
8.8.46: And again when his head was wounded by the fall of her thunderbolt, his blood poured forth; therefrom were born men by thousands.
8.8.47: And Vishnu's Energy struck at this foe with her discus in the battle. Indra's Energy beat that lord of the Asuras with her club.
8.8.48: The world was filled by the thousands of great Asuras, who were his equals, and who sprang from the blood that flowed from him when cloven by the discus of Vishnu's Energy.
8.8.49: Kumara's Energy struck the great Asura Raktavija with her spear, and Varaha's Energy also struck him with her sword, and Maheshvara's Energy with her trident.
8.8.50: And the Daitya Raktavija, that great Asura, filled full of wrath, struck every one of the Mothers in turn with his club.
8.8.51: By the stream of blood, which fell on the earth from him when he received many wounds from the spears, darts and other weapons, Asuras came verily into being in hundreds.
8.8.52: And those Asuras who sprang from that Asura's blood pervaded the whole world; thereat the gods fell into the utmost terror.
8.8.53: Seeing the gods dejected, Chandika spoke with haste; she said to Kali, 'O Chamunda! stretch out thy mouth wide;'
8.8.54: 'with this mouth do thou quickly take in the drops of blood and the great Asuras, which have come into being out of Raktavija at the descent of my weapon on him.'
8.8.55: 'Roam about in the battle, devouring the great Asuras who sprang from him; so shall this Daitya, with his blood ebbing away, meet destruction.'
8.8.56: 'These fierce demons are being devoured by thee, and at the same time no others will be produced.' Having enjoined her thus, the goddess next smote him with her dart.
8.8.57: Kali swallowed Raktavija's blood with her mouth. Then he struck Chandika with his club there;
8.8.58: and the blow of his club caused her no pain, even the slightest, but from his stricken body blood flowed copiously,
8.8.59: and from whatever direction it came, Chamunda takes it then with her mouth. The great Asuras who sprang up from the flow of blood into her mouth,
8.8.60: Chamunda both devoured them and quaffed his blood. The goddess smote Raktavija with her dart, her thunderbolt, arrows, swords and spears,
8.8.61: while Chamunda drank up his blood. Stricken with that multitude of weapons, he fell on the earth's surface,
8.8.62: and the great Asura Raktavija became bloodless, O king. Thereat the thirty gods gained joy unparalleled, O king.
8.8.63: The band of Mothers which sprang from them broke into a dance, being intoxicated with blood.

9.9.2: Wonderful is this that thou, Sir, hast related to me, the majesty of the goddess' exploits in connexion with the slaying of Raktavija;
9.9.3: and I wish to hear further what deed did Shumbha do after Raktavija was killed, and what the very irascible Nishumbha did.
9.9.5: After Raktavija was slain and other demons were killed in the fight, the Asura Shumbha gave way to unbounded wrath, and Nishumbha also.
9.9.6: Pouring out his indignation at beholding his great army being slaughtered, Nishumbha then rushed forward with the flower of the Asura army.
9.9.7: In front of him and behind and on both sides great Asuras, biting their lips and enraged, advanced to slay the goddess.
9.9.8: Shumbha also went forward, mighty in valour, surrounded with his own troops, to slay Chandika in his rage, after engaging in battle with the Mothers.
9.9.9: Then occurred a desperate combat between the goddess and Shumbha and Nishumbha, who both, like two thunder-clouds, rained a most tempestuous shower of arrows on her.
9.9.10: Chandika with multitudes of arrows quickly split the arrows shot by them, and smote the two Asura lords on their limbs with her numerous weapons.
9.9.11: Nishumbha, grasping a sharp scymitar and glittering shield, struck the lion, the noble beast that bore the goddess, on the head.
9.9.12: When her animal was struck, the goddess quickly clove Nishumbha's superb sword with a horse-shoe-shaped arrow, and also his shield on which eight moons were pourtrayed.
9.9.13: When his shield was cloven and his sword too, the Asura hurled his spear; and that his missile also, as it came towards her, she split in two with her discus.
9.9.14: Then Nishumbha, the Danava, puffed up with wrath, seized a dart; and that also, when it came, the goddess shattered with a blow of her fist.
9.9.15: And then, aiming his club, he flung it against Chandika; yet that was shivered by the goddess' trident and became ashes.
9.9.16: As that lordly Daitya then advanced with battle-axe in hand, the goddess struck him with a multitude of arrows and laid him low on the ground.
9.9.17: When his brother Nishumbha, who was terrible in prowess, fell to the ground, Shumbha in utmost fury strode forward to slay Ambika.
9.9.18: And he, standing in his chariot, appeared to fill the entire sky with his eight arms, which were lifted far on high grasping his superb weapons.
9.9.19: Beholding him approaching, the goddess sounded her conch, and made her bow also give forth from its string a note which was exceedingly hard to endure.
9.9.20: And she filled all regions with the clanging of her bell, which caused the vigour of all the Daitya hosts to die away.
9.9.21: Then her lion filled the heaven, the earth and the ten regions of the sky with loud roars, which checked the copious flow of the exudation from the demons' rutting elephants.
9.9.22: Kali, springing upward, then struck the heaven and the earth with both her hands; the boom thereof drowned those previous sounds.
9.9.23: Shivaduti uttered a loud inauspicious laugh. At those sounds the Asuras trembled; Shumbha gave way to utmost rage.
9.9.24: When Ambika cried out 'Stand, O evil-souled! stand!', the gods who had taken their stations in the air then called to her, 'Be thou victorious!'
9.9.25: The spear flaming most terribly, which Shumbha approaching hurled—that, gleaming like a mass of fire as it came along, was driven aside by a great fire-brand.
9.9.26: The vault between the three worlds reverberated with Shumbha's lion-like roaring, but the dreadful sound of the slaughter among his soldiers surpassed that, O king.
9.9.27: The goddess split the arrows shot by Shumbha, and Shumbha the arrows that she discharged, each with her and his sharp arrows in hundreds and thousands.
9.9.28: Chandika, enraged thereat, smote him with a dart. Wounded therewith, he fell in a faint to the ground.
9.9.29: Thereupon Nishumbha, regaining consciousness, seized his bow again and struck the goddess, and Kali and the lion, with arrows.
9.9.30: And the Danava lord, that son of Diti, putting forth a myriad arms, again covered Chandika with a myriad discuses.
9.9.31: The goddess then, enraged—she, Durga who destroys the afflictions of adversity—split those discuses and those arrows with her own arrows.
9.9.32: Then Nishumbha, seizing his club, rushed impetuously at Chandika to slay her outright, with the Daitya host surrounding him.
9.9.33: As he was just falling upon her, Chandika swiftly clove his club with her sharp-edged scymitar. And he took hold of a dart.
9.9.34: Chandika, with a dart hurled swiftly, pierced Nishumbha, the afflicter of the Immortals, in the heart, as he approached with dart in hand.
9.9.35: When he was pierced by the dart, out of his heart issued another man of great strength and great valour, exclaiming 'Stand!'
9.9.36: When he stepped forth, the goddess, laughing aloud, then struck off his head with her scymitar; thereupon he fell to the ground.
9.9.37: The lion then devoured those Asuras whose necks he had crushed with his savage teeth, and Kali and Shivaduti devoured the others.
9.9.38: Some great Asuras perished, being pierced through by the spear held by Kumara's Energy; others were driven back by the water purified by the spell uttered by Brahma's Energy;
9.9.39: and others fell, pierced by the trident wielded by Shiva's Energy; some were pounded to dust on the ground by blows from the snout of Varaha's Energy;
9.9.40: some Danavas were cut to pieces by the discus hurled by Vishnu's Energy; and others again by the thunderbolt discharged from the fingers of Indra's Energy.
9.9.41: Some Asuras perished outright, some fled from the great battle, and others were devoured by Kali, Shivaduti and the lion.

10.10.2: Seeing his brother Nishumbha slain, who was dear to him as his life, and his army being slaughtered, Shumbha in wrath spoke thus:
10.10.3: 'O Durga, who art tainted with the arrogance of strength, bring not thy pride here, thou who, trusting in the strength of the other goddesses, dost fight in exceeding haughtiness!'
10.10.5: Alone verily am I in the world here; what other goddess is there besides me? See, vile one! that these goddesses, who have their divine power from me, are entering into me indeed.
10.10.6: Then all those goddesses, Brahmani and the others, became absorbed into the body of the goddess; Ambika then remained alone indeed.
10.10.8: Whereas I existed with my divine power in many forms here—that has been drawn in by me; truly alone I stand now. Be thou steadfast in combat!
10.10.10: Thereupon commenced a battle between them both, the goddess and Shumbha, while all the gods and the Asuras looked on—a battle without quarter.
10.10.11: With showers of arrows, with sharp weapons and also with pitiless missiles, both engaged anew in a combat which set all the world in fear.
10.10.12: And the lord of the Daityas broke the heavenly missiles, which Ambika discharged in hundreds, with weapons that parried them.
10.10.13: And the supreme goddess in merest play broke the heavenly missiles that he discharged, with fierce shouts, ejaculations and other sounds.
10.10.14: Then the Asura covered the goddess with hundreds of arrows, and the goddess, enraged thereat, split his bow also with her arrows.
10.10.15: And when his bow was split, the lord of the Daityas took up his spear. The goddess split it, as he held it in his hand, with a discus.
10.10.16: Next the supreme monarch of the Daityas, seizing his scymitar and sunlike shield, on which a hundred moons were pourtrayed, rushed at the goddess at that moment.
10.10.17: Just as he was falling upon her, Chandika hastily split his scymitar with sharp arrows shot from her bow, and his shield also which was spotless as the sun's rays; and she felled his steeds, and his chariot together with its charioteer.
10.10.18: With his steeds slain, with his bow split, without a charioteer, the Daitya then grasped his terrible mace, being ready to slay Ambika.
10.10.19: As he was falling upon her, she clove his mace with sharp arrows; nevertheless, raising his fist, he rushed swiftly at her.
10.10.20: The lordly Daitya brought his fist down on the goddess' heart, and the goddess also smote him on his breast with her palm.
10.10.21: Wounded by the blow of her palm, the Daitya king fell suddenly on the earth; and again indeed he rose up,
10.10.22: and springing upward he seized the goddess and mounted on high into the sky. There also Chandika, being without any support, fought with him.
10.10.23: The Daitya and Chandika then fought at first with each other in the sky in a close combat, which wrought dismay among the Siddhas and munis;
10.10.24: after carrying on the close combat for a very long time with him, Ambika lifted him up then and whirled him around and flung him on the earth.
10.10.25: When flung thus he touched the earth, he raised his fist hastily and rushed, evil of soul as he was, with the wish to kill Chandika.
10.10.26: Seeing him, the lord of all the Daitya folk, approaching, the goddess then pierced him in the breast with a dart and felled him down on the earth.
10.10.27: Shattered by the point of the goddess' dart, he fell lifeless on the ground, shaking the whole earth and its seas, islands and mountains.
10.10.28: When that evil-souled demon was slain, the universe became placid, the earth regained perfect well-being, and the sky grew pure.
10.10.29: Portent-clouds, which were full of flame before, became tranquil, and the rivers kept within their channels, when he was stricken down there.
10.10.30: All the bands of gods then grew exceedingly joyful in mind, when he was slain; the Gandharvas sang out sweetly,
10.10.31: and others of them sounded their instruments, and the bevies of Apsarases danced; and favourable breezes blew; very brilliant grew the sun;
10.10.32: and the tranquil sacred fires blazed freely, and tranquil became the strange sounds that had occurred in the regions of the sky.

11.11.2: When the great lord of the Asuras was slain there by the goddess, Indra and the other gods led by Agni offered praise to her, Katyayani, because they had gained their desire; and their faces shone forth like blossoming lotuses, and their hopes became manifest.
11.11.3: O goddess, who removest the sufferings of thy suppliants, be gracious! Be gracious, O mother of the whole world! Be gracious, O queen of the universe; safeguard the universe! Thou, O goddess, art queen of all that is moveable and immoveable!
11.11.4: Thou alone hast become the support of the world, because thou dost subsist in the form of the earth! By thee, who existest in the form of water, all this universe is filled, O thou inviolable in thy valour!
11.11.5: Thou art Vishnu's energy, boundless in thy valour; thou art the germ of the universe, thou art Illusion sublime! All this world has been bewitched, O goddess; thou indeed, when propitious, art the cause of final emancipation on the earth!
11.11.6: All sciences are portions of thee, O goddess; so are all females without exception in the worlds! By thee alone, as mother, this world has been filled! What praise can there be for thee? Thou art beyond praise, the sublimest expression!
11.11.7: When as being the goddess who constitutes every created thing, and who bestows enjoyment and final emancipation, thou art praised—for thy praise again what sublime words can be sufficient?
11.11.8: O thou who abidest under the form of Intelligence in the heart of every living creature; O goddess, who bestowest Svarga and final emancipation, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.9: Thou who, in the form of minutes, moments and other portions of time, dost bring results to pass; O thou who art mighty in the death of the universe, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.10: O thou who art beneficent with every happiness, O lady auspicious, who accomplishest every petition, O giver of refuge, O Tryambaka, O brilliant Gauri, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.11: O eternal goddess, who constitutest the energy of creation, permanence and destruction, O thou abode of good qualities, who consistest of good qualities, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.12: O thou who art devoted to the deliverance of the distressed and afflicted that seek refuge in thee, O goddess who takest away the affliction of all, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.13: O thou who ridest in a heavenly car yoked with swans, who assumest the form of Brahmani, O goddess who sprinklest kusha-grass-steeped water, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.14: O thou who holdest a trident, the moon and a serpent, who art borne on a huge bull, with the natural character of Maheshvari, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.15: O thou who art attended by the peacock and cock, who bearest a great spear, O sinless one; O thou who takest thy station in Kaumari's form, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.16: O thou who holdest as thy finest weapons a conch, discus, club, and the bow Sharnga, be gracious, O thou who hast Vaishnavi's form; O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.17: O thou who graspest a huge formidable discus, who hast uplifted the earth with thy tushes, O auspicious one, who hast a boar-like form, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.18: O thou who in the fierce man-lion form didst put forth thy efforts to slay the Daityas, O thou who art connected with the deliverance of the three worlds, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.19: O thou who hast a diadem and a great thunderbolt, who art dazzling with a thousand eyes, and who tookest away Vritra's life-breath, O Aindri, Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.20: O thou who with the nature of Shivaduti slewest the mighty hosts of the Daityas, O thou of terrible form, of loud shrieks, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.21: O thou who hast a face formidable with tushes, who art decorated with a garland of heads, O Chamunda, who grindest shaven heads, O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.22: O Lakshmi, Modesty, Great Knowledge! O Faith, Nourishment, Svadha, Immoveable! O Great Night, Great Illusion! O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.23: O Mental Vigour, Sarasvati, Choice One! O Welfare, Wife of Babhru, Dark One! O Self-controlled Queen, be thou gracious! O Narayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.24: O thou who hast the nature of all, Queen of all! O thou who possessest the might of all! From terrors save us, O goddess! O goddess Durga, reverence be to thee!
11.11.25: Kindly is this thy countenance, which is adorned with three eyes; may it guard us from all created things! O Katyayani, reverence be to thee!
11.11.26: Formidable with flames, exceedingly sharp, destroying the Asuras without quarter, may thy trident guard us from fear! O Bhadrakali, reverence be to thee!
11.11.27: Thy bell, that fills the world with its ringing and destroys the glories of the Daityas—may that bell guard us, O goddess, even us like children, from sins!
11.11.28: Besmirched with the blood and fat of the Asuras as with mire, gleaming with rays in thy hand—may thy scymitar be for our welfare! O Chandika, to thee we bow!
11.11.29: Thou destroyest all sicknesses, when gratified; but when wrathful, destroyest all longed-for desires. No calamity befalls men who have sought unto thee! They who have sought unto thee become verily a refuge themselves!
11.11.30: This slaughter that thou hast now wrought on the great Asuras who hate righteousness, O goddess, by multiplying thy body in many forms—O Ambika, what other goddess achieves that?
11.11.31: In the sciences, in the scriptures, which need the lamp of discrimination, and in the ancient sayings, who but thou, within the pit of selfishness, wherein is exceeding great darkness, causes this universe to whirl about most grievously?
11.11.32: Wherever dwell Rakshasas and virulently-poisonous Nagas, wherever foes exist, wherever the powers of the Dasyus, and where flaming fire appears amid the ocean, there abiding thou dost safeguard the universe!
11.11.33: O queen of the universe, thou safeguardest the universe! Thou hast the nature of the universe, for thou upholdest the universe. Thou art the lady worthy to be praised by the lord of the universe. They are the refuge of the universe, who bow in faith before thee!
11.11.34: O goddess, be gracious! Protect us wholly from fear of our foes perpetually, as thou hast at this very time saved us promptly by the slaughter of the Asuras! And bring thou quickly to rest the sins of all the worlds and the great calamities which have sprung from the maturing of portents!
11.11.35: To us who are prostrate be thou gracious, O goddess, who takest away affliction from the universe! O thou worthy of praise from the dwellers in the three worlds, bestow thou boons on the worlds!
11.11.37: I am ready to bestow a boon. O ye hosts of gods, choose whatever boon ye desire in your mind; I grant it as a thing that benefits the worlds.
11.11.39: O queen of all, complete thou thus indeed the pacification of every trouble of the three worlds, and the destruction of our enemies.
11.11.41: When the twenty-eighth age has arrived, in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, two other great Asuras shall be born, Shumbha and Nishumbha.
11.11.42: Then, born as the offspring of Yashoda's womb in the cowherd Nanda's house, and dwelling on the Vindhya mountains, I will destroy them both.
11.11.43: And again, becoming incarnate in a very terrible form on the face of the earth, I will slay the Vaiprachitta Danavas;
